governanceNotes: Authored conservatively as ASSOCIATION_ONLY: the alkaline-reflux literature documents duodenogastric bile reflux producing gastritis and esophagitis in the same patients and describes a shared postsurgical dysmotility environment, but the classic evidence base is postsurgical observational series where anteceding gastroduodenal surgery is the dominant driver, so no directional bile-reflux-to-esophagitis causal claim is asserted for non-surgical or individual cases.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The alkaline (enterogastric) reflux literature documents bile-containing reflux producing both gastritis and esophagitis: a review of alkaline reflux gastritis and esophagitis describes the syndrome and its association with gastroduodenal dysmotility and prior gastric surgery, and a surgical series of spontaneous enterogastric reflux reported gastritis and esophagitis occurring together in refluxing patients; bile reflux is also frequently documented alongside acid reflux in reflux-type esophagitis cohorts.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level for this edge: the strongest published associations come from postsurgical populations where the operation itself created the reflux, non-surgical bile reflux cohorts are small and frequently confounded by concurrent acid reflux, H. pylori status, NSAID exposure, and motility disorders that independently injure the esophageal mucosa, and the relative contribution of the biliary component alone cannot be isolated for any individual, so the mapping asserts syndrome-level co-occurrence only.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized biliary-mucosal-injury pathway has been described: duodenogastric reflux exposes the gastric and distal esophageal mucosa to bile acids and lysolecithin, which are membrane-detergent agents that disrupt the mucus barrier and can induce epithelial inflammation in experimental settings; in the postsurgical stomach, loss of the pyloric barrier plus antrectomy-related dysmotility permits sustained alkaline exposure that produced the gastritis-esophagitis syndrome in the classic series. Because the published cohorts cannot separate the biliary fraction from concurrent acid injury, this cascade explains co-occurrence without establishing that bile reflux caused esophagitis in any individual case, and iatrogenic postsurgical etiology remains the dominant alternative explanation.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Bile-containing reflux and esophageal inflammation co-occur in published series, but individual determination requires gastroscopic and histologic documentation of both conditions with chronology, quantification of the biliary (non-acid) reflux fraction where available, and exclusion of acid-driven, medication-related, and postsurgical explanations, all reviewed case by case by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Endoscopic and histologic confirmation of bile reflux gastritis (including bile-staining and gastritis pattern) and of esophagitis with grade documentation; chronology between the two diagnoses; objective bile-reflux quantification (e.g., Bilitec or impedance-pH monitoring) distinguishing non-acid from acid reflux; medication and surgical history review; a medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Prior gastrectomy, vagotomy, or bariatric surgery as the iatrogenic source of both bile reflux and esophagitis
Conventional acid (GERD-driven) esophagitis with incidental bile co-reflux
H. pylori-associated gastritis or NSAID/medication injury as the primary mucosal insult
Primary esophageal motility disorder or impaired lower-esophageal-sphincter function driving reflux independent of the biliary component

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: the bile-acid detergent injury model is biologically coherent and the gastritis-esophagitis co-occurrence is documented, but the evidence base cannot isolate the biliary fraction from acid and postsurgical drivers, so this edge flags the comorbidity for evidence-gap review only and must never be presented as established causation or aggravation.
evidenceGaps: Endoscopically and histologically documented bile reflux gastritis with date
Documented esophagitis with grade and chronology relative to the gastritis
Objective non-acid (biliary) reflux quantification where available
A medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case

sourceReferences.citation: Nath BJ, Warshaw AL. Alkaline reflux gastritis and esophagitis. Annu Rev Med. 1984;35:383-396. PMID 6372664. doi:10.1146/annurev.me.35.020184.002123.
sourceReferences.note: Review describing the alkaline reflux syndrome in which duodenogastric bile-containing reflux produces gastritis and esophagitis, principally in the postsurgical setting; supports the syndrome-level co-occurrence proposition and the postsurgical-confound caution, not a directional claim for non-surgical cases.
